title: White House Demands Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle Resign, Says New Trump Press Secretary – CNBC Report
body:
Washington’s executive office has formally requested that Kimberly Guilfoyle, the United States ambassador to Greece, step down from her post, according to a statement delivered by new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday. The request, which marks one of the first high‑profile personnel moves of the Biden administration’s second year, underscores growing tensions within the diplomatic corps and raises questions about the administration’s broader strategy for managing its overseas appointments.

Guilfoyle, a former television personality and longtime political operative, was appointed to the Athens embassy in 2022 after a career that included roles on the campaign trail for former President Donald Trump and a stint as a senior adviser on the 2020 transition team. Her tenure in Greece has been marked by a series of public disagreements with senior State Department officials over policy priorities, ranging from energy security to the handling of migration flows across the Aegean. Critics within the diplomatic community have also noted her limited experience in traditional diplomatic channels, describing her approach as “politically driven” rather than “institutionally grounded.”

The decision to ask for her resignation comes amid a broader effort by the White House to recalibrate its foreign policy team after a year of heightened geopolitical challenges, including the war in Ukraine, strained relations with China, and a resurgence of regional instability in the Eastern Mediterranean. Officials close to the administration have indicated that the move is intended to restore confidence in the embassy’s ability to coordinate effectively with both Washington and Athens, especially as Greece plays a pivotal role in NATO’s southern flank and in the EU’s energy diversification plans. By replacing an ambassador whose public profile has often eclipsed her diplomatic duties, the administration hopes to signal a renewed commitment to professional expertise and multilateral cooperation.

State Department insiders say the resignation request was not a sudden development but the culmination of months of internal reviews and private consultations. A senior diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that “the ambassador’s public statements on issues such as the Cyprus dispute and Turkey’s naval activities have at times diverged from the official U.S. position, creating friction with our regional partners.” The same source added that the administration had been exploring a replacement who would possess a deeper background in European affairs and a track record of navigating complex alliance dynamics.

Political analysts view the episode as a litmus test for the Biden administration’s handling of politically appointed ambassadors, a category that has traditionally included donors, former legislators, and campaign veterans. While such appointments can bring valuable domestic connections, they also risk compromising the perceived neutrality and effectiveness of U.S. diplomatic missions. Professor Elena Marquez, a specialist in American foreign policy at Georgetown University, remarked, “The Guilfoyle case illustrates the delicate balance between rewarding political loyalty and ensuring that our overseas representatives have the requisite skill set to manage nuanced, often volatile, regional issues.” She warned that future administrations might need to adopt stricter vetting procedures to avoid similar mismatches.

The White House has not disclosed who will assume the ambassadorial duties on an interim basis, but a senior official indicated that a career foreign service officer is likely to step in as chargé d’affaires while a permanent replacement is identified. The administration has also signaled that it will prioritize candidates with extensive experience in European security matters and a demonstrated ability to work collaboratively with both NATO allies and regional partners.

As the United States continues to navigate a complex international landscape, the resignation request for Ambassador Guilfoyle serves as a reminder that diplomatic appointments are more than symbolic gestures; they are critical instruments of policy execution. The coming weeks will reveal how quickly Washington can install a successor capable of strengthening the U.S.–Greece partnership and reinforcing broader strategic objectives in a region where stability remains fragile. The outcome will likely shape not only bilateral ties but also the administration’s broader approach to aligning political appointments with the professional demands of modern diplomacy.
